Bohdan Kucheriavyi: Ever since I started covering Tesla

here on Seeking Alpha, I've been skeptical that robotaxis will be as good for the rideshare business as some investors expect. The main reason for that is the company that develops the driving software also controls where its rides get sold, while the app itself can be replaced.
Take what's been going on between Waymo
and Uber

. The two ran a pilot in Phoenix for almost three years, and it quietly ended this spring with Waymo folding the cars back into its own fleet. It's also been confirmed that Waymo plans to launch its own app in Austin and Atlanta in January 2028, a few months before its contract with Uber runs out. That makes sense from Waymo's perspective since it already serves riders directly in most of its other cities.
Considering this, the question for me is not which platform benefits from robotaxis, but which one can survive a partner walking away.
At this point, Uber
looks better prepared than the other two, mostly because it has not tied itself to a single autonomous driving company. The company says it has more than 20 AV partners, including Zoox
and Motional. It's also an investor in WeRide
. Lyft
and Grab
are trying something similar with Waymo in Nashville and WeRide in Singapore, but on a much smaller scale.

It's also important to remember that Waymo is the leader in this business, and the Alphabet segment that houses it lost $1.8B in Q2 alone. That's why I'm not willing to pay a premium for the robotaxi plans of any rideshare company right now, even though Uber
remains the most reasonable option of the three if someone wants exposure to this theme.
Simple Investment Ideas: While I expect all the major rideshare companies to experience margin compression as robotaxis gain traction, I expect Uber
to adapt well as a result of its established partnerships, operations, size, and the network effects that come along with it.
I am highly skeptical of Tesla's

vision-dominant robotaxi tech stack, as all evidence points to the fact that AI is nowhere near ready for the vision-centric approach Tesla is taking. Just because a human brain can do it does not mean a ~5 billion parameter model running in a couple of GPUs can do it.
Waymo
, on the other hand, has a far better tech stack (lidar, etc.) to approach the robotaxi problem and is proving out its case to a large degree, given its explosive growth in recent years.
Ricardo Fernandez: Uber
is by far the best ride-hail stock for the developing robotaxi or autonomous vehicle ecosystem.
As I understand it, Uber will move from the sharing economy to owning the assets. It will replace, regulation permitting, the owner-operator with its own robotaxi. Whether it is made by Nio
or Rivian
and/or uses Pony AI
or WeRide
AV tech, Uber should capture the lion's share of the fare and manage the fleet to generate high returns almost immediately. This is made possible by the existing 200M active customers.
The robotaxi promises to be more than 3x more productive than a human driver. Thus, plugging it into the Uber
ride-hail platform can generate exceptional returns, which I discussed in my Uber reports.
